title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
claim: A model that denoises a scrambled set of parts into valid structures can be adapted, with little data, to reconstruct objects from images.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right; noisy pile connected by curves to denoised outputs
description: A rendered LEGO scene in two rows. The top row has a central pile of loose yellow and red bricks. Thin gray curves connect the pile to several translucent gray ghost assemblies. These show noisy poses. Each ghost assembly leads to a solid, finished yellow-and-red duck or animal on the left and right. The curves show a noisy-to-clean denoising mapping from one pile to many valid structures. The bottom row starts with a photo of a yellow dump truck on an easel at the far left. Next is a pile of black tires, yellow and black pieces, and a translucent partly assembled truck. At the far right is a finished yellow dump truck. Orange and black curves link the stages. The eye goes first to the colorful central brick pile and the animals around it. Beyond the caption, the figure has no text labels.
caption: Top: We present BrickFlow, an SE(3) flow-matching model trained to take in a known set of LEGO pieces (pile) with noisy poses (translucent) and denoise them into some valid structure. Bottom: Using a procedural dataset 1% the size, we adapt it for image-conditioned reconstruction.
abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/
